prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks based on magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms

statement.case_for: I opened with B013 first and B015 fourth, and I move B015 to the top after reading the ballots. It meets the test I apply to every candidate: an original invention (Katori's magic-wavelength lattice, 2001-03), followed by a demonstrated realization (first strontium lattice clocks, then Ye's JILA systems pushing fractional uncertainty to the 1e-18 level), independently reproduced in many national laboratories and intercompared at that precision. Like the instruments I work with, it opens a door: tests of constants and of gravitational redshift, relativistic geodesy, and the pending redefinition of the second. It is also the only candidate that all eight of us ranked, with five placing it in the top three and two placing it first. The two-person credit is clean and reflects idea plus realization, which is the kind of attribution I can state with confidence.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that the prize already honoured optical frequency-comb metrology in 2005 and ion-clock work (Wineland, 2012), so some will see lattice clocks as an incremental extension of precision timekeeping rather than a new discovery. Other laboratories (for example PTB and NIST) ran parallel clock efforts, and ion clocks reach comparable accuracy, so the committee must be sure that magic-wavelength trapping is the decisive original contribution and that Katori and Ye are the right two. The redefinition of the second has not yet happened, so the societal benefit is still prospective.

responses.point: Kroll ranks the lattice clock first as a mature, reproduced measurement advance with a clean Katori and Ye split between the idea and the performance record.
responses.response: I agree on maturity and on the two-name configuration. I would add that we should keep the original contribution separate from the later one: Katori's magic-wavelength proposal and early Sr clocks are the invention, while Ye's record accuracy is excellent but partly later and more beautiful work. I accept the pairing because Ye's group also demonstrated the clock operating regime that proved the concept at the 1e-18 level, but the citation should name the lattice scheme and not just 'precision'. I do not follow Kroll in ranking atom interferometry second, because credit there is spread over Pritchard, Chu, Kasevich and Mlynek, and the Chu part was partly covered in 1997.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks IceCube first as a genuine new window with several independent confirmations (diffuse flux, TXS 0506+056, NGC 1068) and the instrument itself as a bold concept.
responses.response: I share the view that a cubic-kilometre detector in ice is an instrument that opened a door, and it is my second choice and an alternative here. My difficulty is attribution: the discovery paper rests on a collaboration of hundreds, and Spiering's role lies in the Baikal and AMANDA lineage, whereas I only credited Halzen and Karle. Danielsson's three names are historically more complete, but then DUMAND, Baikal and AMANDA pioneers are not credited. Until we are 'absolutely sure' about who did the original work, I cannot put B007 ahead of a case where the originators are unambiguous.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene first, as a minimal continuum model followed by experiments that found correlated states exactly at the predicted angle.
responses.response: The theory-then-experiment sequence is persuasive and I ranked it third. My reservations are that the origin of the superconductivity is still debated, sample-to-sample variation is large, and the experimental first author (Yuan Cao) is not among the three credited names, so the history of who did the original experiment is not fully captured by the list. I think a few more years of settled mechanism would make the case stronger. I would not stand in the way if the committee finds that the discovery itself, as distinct from its interpretation, is secure.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED first as the architecture of nearly all superconducting quantum processors, with Blais, Wallraff and Schoelkopf as the three names, while admitting Girvin, Huang and Majer are not on the entry.
responses.response: I ranked it sixth for two reasons Johansson himself raises: the credit boundary around the 2004 proposal and experiment is unusually crowded, and the 2025 prize for macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits is close enough that a second superconducting-circuit award so soon seems premature. I recognise the technological importance, but importance as an architecture is not the same as the original discovery. I also note that we are colleagues in neighbouring Chalmers groups, so I am especially careful not to lean on his field in either direction.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks B013 sixth, below the topological and moire candidates, while still proposing Rose, Haider and Urban if it is considered.
responses.response: I appreciate that Eriksson supports the same three names. I accept that B013 attracted only three rankings, and I will say plainly that this is my own field, so I discount my first-place ranking. The scientific case remains that aberration correction broke a limit that held for sixty years, and Rose (design), Haider (hexapole corrector) and Urban (demonstration) are an unusually clean attribution. But the committee should weigh Krivanek and Dellby for the STEM corrector, and I do not think the discussion yet shows a wide enough view to place B013 above lattice clocks.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards optical lattice clocks as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 frequency-comb and 2012 ion-control prizes.
Whether Ye's contribution is best framed as an original invention or as a later, higher-performance realization of Katori's scheme.
For B013, whether Krivanek and Dellby (aberration-corrected STEM) must be credited alongside Rose, Haider and Urban, which would exceed three names.
For B007, whether a three-name credit can be defended against the AMANDA and Baikal lineage and the scale of the IceCube collaboration.
statement.conflict_note: I am a transmission electron microscopist at Chalmers, so the electron-optics ballot B013 lies in my own field and I may need to recuse myself from a decision on it, and I discount my own first-place ranking of it accordingly. Göran Johansson, who ranks B024 first, is a colleague in the Chalmers Physics department, which is a mild institutional connection. I have no specific connection to the lattice clock candidates Katori and Ye.
